newsitem.title: USA: Businessman testifies about campaign contribution.
newsitem.headline: Businessman testifies about campaign contribution.

text.p: A federal grand jury investigating campaign fund-raising heard testimony from a businessman Wednesday on his talks with President Clinton and a top White House aide about a Democratic Party contribution.

Florida businessman R. Warren Medoff said he was called to testify before the secret grand jury proceeding about "campaign finances and a contribution regarding the president, the White House and the Democratic National Committee."

A federal grand jury, under the direction of a Justice Department task force, has been hearing testimony for about a month involving possibly illegal campaign contributions to the Democrats during last year's election.

Medoff's appearance gave the first confirmation the task force is investigating his dealings with former Deputy White House Chief of Staff Harold Ickes. It was not known what possible violation of the law prosecutors were examining.

After testifying for 2-1/2 hours under oath, Medoff recounted for reporters his brief conversation with Clinton Oct. 22 at a Florida fundraiser in which he mainly discussed humanitarian help to hurricane victims.

Medoff has said that he wrote on the back of one of his business cards: "My associate has $5 million he wants to contribute to your campaign." A few days later, he said, Ickes called him at his office concerning "a possible donation on behalf of my associate in Texas."

He said Ickes then faxed him from the White House a memo directing that $500,000 be sent to the Democratic National Committee. The White House has acknowledged that its fax machine and telephone line should not have been used for fund-raising.
Medoff has said Ickes told him to shred the memo. Ickes has denied that but has said he may have told Medoff it was "inoperative."
Medoff said he "went over written documents and events" concerning Ickes with the grand jury. "The bulk of the time was spent" on his dealings with Ickes, he said.

Asked if anything illegal or improper occurred, Medoff said: "Obviously, when a grand jury is convened, there's some question of legality." But he said no one at the White House "offered any form of inducement" for the contribution.

After Democratic party officials raised questions, no contribution was ever made by Medoff's associate, Texas businessman William Morgan, who also was summoned before the grand jury Wednesday but refused to comment to reporters.

Medoff, who was subpoenaed to testify, said prosecutors told him he had been called as a witness, not as a target of the investigation. He said prosecutors had subpoenaed as many as 90 pages of documents, primarily dealing with Ickes, and requested more documents. He said he was cooperating with the probe.
